en: Yuanzhao extinguished the broken sand-pot; Xiyuan was truly outstanding. His five assemblies of public teachings were all personally edited and finalized by him, leaving nothing that could be discarded.

What is called "transcending the school and exceeding the standard," "cutting through iron and chopping through nails"—the phrase that blinds the eyes of even the most seasoned monks—is found beyond this record.
Those who read it must take care not to miss it. I and... [text ends]
Yanxian was my closest friend. I was just about to trouble Yanxian with these words, yet Yanxian has first troubled me. How tragic!
Written respectfully by Huanghai Yuanzhao, resident of Yuyang Monastery, during the middle spring of the Guihai year of the Jingding era.

The Recorded Sayings of West Rock Master (Xiyán Heshàng) while Residing at Dìnghuì Chándì Temple in Píngjiāng Prefecture, Compiled by His Disciples Xiūyì and Others.
Holding fast to Mount Jízú, he rushed to Mount Huángméi; in all this, not a single point was involved. Why?
Therefore, the tiger’s body is originally striped.
Ascending the seat, he held up the incense and said: "This one portion of incense, offered into the burner, I respectfully present to extend blessings to the present Emperor, praying for his person:
ten thousand years, ten thousand years, ten thousand times ten thousand years! Next, holding up the incense, he said: This one portion..."
[Incense] is offered on behalf of the Chancellor of the Prefecture, the Great Minister, and all the dignitaries of the district, to increase their years of official service.
Again, he holds up the incense and says: "This single portion of incense, being government property, I dare not trade privately.
I burn it within this burner to offer to the Great Master Chan Master Fojian, currently residing at Mount Jing, in gratitude for the milk of the Dharma."
Ascending the hall for the Buddha-Bathing ceremony: Conceived in the womb, he was not attached; one error leads to a hundred errors.
Walking seven steps, he brought dust upon himself, and even until this very day, it cannot be shaken off. It cannot be shaken off! Wisdom and Samādhi can only follow the error with what is mistaken.
Picking up a three-catty handleless ladle—(he strikes the meditation staff once)—and descends from the seat.

On the Mid-Autumn Festival, [the Master] took his seat after dismissing the administrative staff. (Holding up his staff, he looked around and said: "When an object meets its master, the eye stands firm and upright. This is the moon-repairing axe of our house;
it must be held up together by the collective strength of the assembly. Where there is no deficiency, there is still room for repair."
Since the great assembly is already without fullness or deficiency, what more is there to repair?
If you can understand this—(claps the table once)—then right now the axe-handle has sprouted flowers. If it is otherwise—(leans on his staff)—then listen as I ascend the hall:
"Every step taken gives rise to thorns; every turn of the body falls into a precipice. Without moving so much as a single hair, one is liberated right where one is."
Sunken and buried. Hūṃ hūṃ! How utterly intolerable! At the crossroads, he acts like one driven by wind or madness. The old fellow Puhua declared:
"Tomorrow there is a vegetarian feast at the Great Compassion Temple."
Ascending the hall: "One does not adjust one's cap beneath a plum tree; one does not tuck in one's shoes in a melon patch. How vexing is that old barbarian from the West!

Having traveled a hundred thousand *li* to the East, he has left the people of China in a state of doubt. They thought it was a single-lineage transmission and a direct pointing [to the human heart]. (He strikes the meditation seat. Nine times nine is originally eighty-two.
Opening the furnace, he ascends the hall. Danxia burned several wooden Buddhas to ward off the bitter cold;
Fachang gathered eighteen Arhats to sit around the hearth in meditation. One brings forth a bountiful year; the other gives rise to unfiliality.
The ancients acted thus, yet their wisdom and concentration were not thus. (He strikes the staff once. What is it? Beans bursting in cold ashes.

Because the Prefectural Office sent officials to the temple to conduct a joint investigation, I retired from the monastery to ascend the hall. The great earth has become a prison, where Buddhas and Patriarchs are interrogated;
the records of their confessions remain incomplete, while blows and shouts fall like thunder and rain. Innocently, this has brought trouble upon this mountain monk.

Where there is grievance, there is no place for vindication. Yet, where there is a place for vindication, one should shoulder the knotted staff across one’s back, heedless of others, and go straight into a thousand peaks and ten thousand peaks.
The Recorded Sayings of Nengren Chan Monastery at Yanshan, Wenzhou, compiled by his disciples Xiuyi and others. [At the] Mountain Gate:
(Looking over the assembly) Do you understand? If you do not, then for now turn toward the secondary gate and join with all of you...
People have come to meet one another.
At the Abbot’s quarters, this is a land of lips and teeth, a kingdom of throats; today, it is all at once cut off, with not even a hair’s breadth of leakage.
It has become so that throughout the four quarters and eight directions, the wind blows whistling; is there anyone who would climb the mountains to present tribute?

Regarding the Dharma seat: its establishment at the gate and courtyard is certainly not without precedent. As for Sumeru-dīpa-rāja, though his discourse on entering the principle is profound, he still falls one degree short of this mountain monk.

In the *Xiǎocān* (Small Sermon), [the Master] raised the "Sleeping Dragon" case and took up his staff, saying: "This old monk has lived in the mountains for thirty years, and it is only now that I have obtained this staff."
"Vitality. Suddenly, a monk stepped forward and asked, "Master, what vitality did you obtain from him? Long said, "Crossing streams and crossing ridges;

leaning eastward and leaning westward. (The Master commented: "Sleeping Dragon Monk claimed for himself that after thirty years of dwelling in the mountains, he had mastered the vitality of the staff.
Yet, when pressed lightly by this monk, he was completely uprooted, expending all that much vitality for nothing."
Power. I did not know where this master staff was. Today, as I have newly settled upon this mountain, I too have obtained the power of this master staff.

But tell me, what kind of power have I obtained? (Leans on the staff. Having finished his discourse, he descends from the seat to thank the newly appointed Chief Librarian and the two classes of long-standing administrative officers.
He ascends the hall again and says: "I, this mountain monk, carry a single shoulder-load of Buddha-dharma and Zen."
The Way has already flown away into the borders of West State.
Since entering the borders of East State, while in a state of non-mindfulness, I happened upon a single phrase that none of the Buddhas or Patriarchs of antiquity had ever reached.

I have harbored it within my breast as I traveled through three states and four counties, never lightly bringing it forth. Now that I have entered this monastery and human affairs have settled, [I may speak of it].
I cannot avoid beating the drum and ascending the hall to present this to all of you, so that everyone may hear it and each of you shall rejoice and leap for joy, exclaiming, "How unprecedented!
But tell me, which is that one phrase? [The official] on the east side; the head monk on the west side.
Small Sermon for the Summer Retreat. To truly uphold and proclaim [the Dharma], one must leave no trace for forty-nine days.
Although the formal retreat according to the regulations lasts for one hundred and twenty days, that is not yet considered a long term.

Today, Śākyamuni opens a single thread of the path, so that his eyebrows may entwine with those of all people as we dwell together in this summer retreat. We shall simply take ten days as a decade and ninety days as a summer. Together...
Sharing a basket with rice; sharing a dream and a bed; sharing the cool when it is cool and the heat when it is hot; walking together on the path by the stream when there is nothing to do;
sometimes gazing together at the mountain above the house—it is indeed shared in these ways. Yet, as for the large and small stones within the mountains...
In the end, how many are there? (He raises his staff and strikes the ground once. "Three before and three after.
Secretary Xie Yuan and Master Miaozang held the whisk; the Head of the Monastery managed the summer retreat feast and presided over the drawing of lots.

Ascending the hall: The mystery within mysteries, the marvel within marvels. To recognize its source and origin, and to grasp its pivotal essence—Puhua kicked over the rice table, and Shuilao let out a great laugh.
But tell me, what was he laughing at? A gambler’s luck runs out at the gambling den.
Ascending the hall, he called to the assembly, saying: "Yesterday, when I reached the entrance of the mountain gate, I saw two newly arrived monks.
I then asked one of them, 'Where have you come from, Venerable? The monk replied, 'I have come from the foot of Che-ling.'"
He then asked him, "Where is the cart? The man immediately made the gesture of pushing a cart.
He then asked a newly arrived monk, "Elder, from which direction have you come? The monk said, "I have come from the side of Yueqing. He then asked him, "Where is Yueqing?
The man immediately made the gesture of playing music. At that time, the mountain monk’s questions were identical in both cases, yet the two men’s responses were likewise so.
They appear similar. Yet, between them, one person possesses some backbone, while the other has none at all.
When I, this mountain monk, speak thus, can you all discern the difference? If you cannot discern it, I shall not begrudge my speech and will explain it clearly for you:
who has some backbone and who has none at all. Today is the first [day].
1. On the second day of the month, he ascended the hall:
The mountains are empty and the trees have shed their leaves; the autumn is clear and the dew is cold. Śākyamuni was crude and hasty; Bodhidharma was muddled and vague.
Only Tao Qianjing, at his eastern fence, plucks the yellow chrysanthemums, drunk to the dregs of the setting sun.

Ascending the hall for the Buddha-bath ceremony: pointing with both hands to heaven and earth, he walks about even more. How pitiable is the Yellow-faced Old Man—like a crab falling into a boiling cauldron!
Ascending the hall for the opening of the furnace: "The assembly, there is the monk but no hall; there is the furnace but no fire. The mountain monk’s skills are exhausted. He asks:
"Take up the wooden senior monk. (He brandishes his staff. "Wooden senior monk, since wood can produce fire, why does it not produce a little for you all as an offering?
(He strikes the ground with the staff and says: "It would burn to death the foolish old Zhaozhou; it would freeze to death the broken stove at Mount Songshan."
The Buddha ascends the hall for the Nirvana assembly: An old rebel spirit who has overturned heaven and earth; the Heavenly Teacher transformed fire to burn his own body.
A rebel mind and rebel conduct are difficult to extinguish; in the second month, it remains as the middle spring as before.
Ascending the hall for the Buddha-bath ceremony, he addressed the assembly, saying: "When a single grain of tares or weeds is sown, its harm is not yet apparent.
Yet, given time and nurtured by dew and rain, there is none that does not grow luxuriantly to become a thief to the abundant harvest."
Throughout the monasteries of the world, from antiquity to the present, on this very month, this very day, and at this very hour, incense-water and ink-juice are black;
fragrant rice and ink are pitch-black; prostrations have worn through the knees and shins; and the smoke of the censers fills the air to suffocation. Thieves! Thieves!
Small Sermon for the Summer Retreat: The nation has no sword to quell disorder; the entire country is at peace. The household has no chart of Baize;
the whole family is blessed with good fortune. Taking Great Perfect Enlightenment as my monastery, body and mind dwell in tranquility, the wisdom of universal equality.
Calamity arises from affairs; the Dharma emerges and the wicked are born. From the Eastern Land to the Western Region, there are wax figures and iron pellets.

One distinguishes between upper, middle, and lower seats, and establishes long and short periods of retreat. To the shackles already upon one’s head, one adds further shackles; to the cangues already at one’s side, one fastens yet more cangues.

How can it compare to the ever-present clouds soaring ten thousand fathoms high, and the flying waterfalls thundering from a thousand spans? Beside the Bridge of the Compassionate Vessel, the moon in the water and the moonlight intermingle;
before the Hall of No-Speech, the warm breeze enters as a musical offering. Now tell me: within this, is there still any principle of the Buddha-dharma or not?
Though the days of the millennium calendar may be of no use, if one transgresses them, I must teach that their entire lineage be extinguished.
Ascending the hall, he thanked the five who had held the whisk. One, two, three, four, five— They do not fall within the notes of gong, shang, jue, zhi, or yu.
Their harmonious style transcends a thousand ages; How could "White Snow" or "Yangchun" ever suffice to count against it? Who nowadays would take pleasure in hearing this melody?
Last night the moon hung over the tall pines.
On the Dragon Boat Festival, he ascended the hall and called to the assembly, saying: "Grand Master Chu! (He raises his whisk) This very thing is it.
He claimed to be the only one sober; who knew he was the only one drunk? No one in the entire world can pry it loose, and even this mountain monk is helpless against it. Not so.
"Exempting the Sichuan dialect for this turn of duty, I shall sing a *Chuci* poem to depart. (After a long pause, he says: "Did you hear it?
Just now it was like the Lord of Xiang; now, however, it has become a mountain ghost."
Upon receiving the news of the passing of Master Wuzhun of Mount Jing, he held up incense and said:
"On the first day of the third month, this old fellow ascended the hall and shook out that which cannot be spoken; it was a thief’s loot.
It was only because for one period of time I had not shaken it all out, that Nengren had to burn incense with his left hand. Why is this so? A whole sheep inside a honeycomb."
The Small Precept for the End of the Summer Retreat. For ninety days one restrains the feet, and for three months one dwells in seclusion.
Taking up the Bodhisattva vehicle and practicing the path of quiescence—such talk is often found among ordinary people.

But as for this mountain monk, throughout this summer I have been occupied with earth and wood, moving back and forth between the eastern and western corridors, climbing up and down until my two feet have grown sores. What feet do I have to restrain?
Yet it may be restrained. Piles of years and pits, ten thousand fathoms on all four sides; demonic cities in many layers. Little joy and much anger;

thorns in the morning and brambles in the evening. What dwelling could there be that is secure? And what vehicle of the Bodhisattvas is there to rely upon? What practice of quiescent extinction is there to cultivate?

Nevertheless, though this be so, you people have not spent this summer in vain. As for me, the mountain monk, this summer— (Note: The text ends abruptly. The final phrase "As for me, the mountain monk, this summer—" suggests a continuation, likely contrasting his own realization with the listeners' lack of progress.)
It is not in vain either. While others take a wax figure as their test, this mountain monk also takes a wax figure as his test.
The wax figure is ice. Now tell me: does the test lie with you, or does it lie with this mountain monk? A thousand peaks pay homage to Mount Hua;
ten thousand streams flow solemnly into the vast ocean.
Ascending the hall on the Double Ninth: Heaven is high and earth is thick; the moon is for the night, the sun is for the day. The Double Ninth is surely the ninth day of the ninth month.
Yuanming plucks chrysanthemums facing the eastern hedge; the mountain monk faces south and gazes at the Big Dipper.

Ascending the hall, the Master raised the following case: A monk asked Yunmen, "What is it like when the trees wither and the leaves fall? Yunmen said, "The essence is revealed in its entirety. The Master commented:
"Master Yunmen creates a track where there was no track; he creates a path of meaning where there was no path of meaning. I, Nengren, am not like this.
When the trees wither and the leaves fall, the birds in their nests first see the sun, and the ants in their holes [sense the change]."
Not Knowing Cold.
Compiled by the attendants Jingyuan and others from the Discourse Record of Donglin Chan Temple in Jiangzhou.
The Mountain Gate faces the green mountains; the gate stands upon an ancient path. Were it not for Tao Yuanming, he would have knit his brows and turned back.
Today, this mountain monk suppresses his majestic brilliance and leads you all forward for two or three steps.
The Abbot’s quarters: four sevens and two threes. Nailing down the stake and rocking the oars—this was the ancient ancestor Ying’an. Untying the moorings and setting sail—this is the new Donglin.
Turning the prow of the boat, the wind is high and the waters swift; ten thousand miles and a hundred thousand leagues in a single instant.

He requested the Head Seat, Yuan, to ascend the hall to establish the monastic lineage. With hands and feet flailing in all directions, three heads and two faces, this joyous adversary is encountered at every turn.
This mountain monk establishes the fundamental tenets; you must act for me to bring them to completion.
The student has not yet reached the source, and thus requests the Master’s skillful means. Whether there are skillful means or no skillful means—Shigong drew his bow. Three.
Hitting the mark with an arrow.
On the winter solstice, during the small *sīmān* (small-scale teaching), he summoned the assembly and said: "Each and every one of you possesses, beneath your robes and bowls, a calendar of no-words.
Within it are the seventy-two seasonal signs, the twenty-four solar energies, the varying lengths of the months, and the intercalary days of the year."
Each and every part is clearly manifest; for what reason do you not simply look directly at it with your own eyes?

Instead, you have needlessly thrown yourself into confusion regarding the sixty-year cycle of the sexagenary calendar, only to come here to listen to the mountain monk’s words. For three winters and nine summers, how truly a great waste this has been!

Although this mountain monk certainly does not wield the power over yin and yang, nor does he possess the hand that can manipulate the workings of creation, tonight I cannot help but try to test [your understanding] with you all.
"Person. He points to this text and departs. (With his whisk, he strikes the left side of the meditation seat and says:

"Yang is the gentleman. (He strikes the right side and says: "Yin is the petty man. (He draws a single line across the middle and says: "The way of the gentleman grows; the way of the petty man wanes.
The dragon roars from the withered tree; the tiger bellows in the level forest. (East Lin has these two plaques. Even so, it is thus.
Just as there are ten thousand layers of Mount Lu before our eyes, from antiquity to the present, with the south of the mountain called "Yang" (sunlight) and the north called "Yin" (shade)—
can you here explain the principle of waxing and waning? (A shout) You disciples of Sun Bin, beware of prying into the tortoise shell!
Again, he cites this case: A monk came to visit Muzhou. Muzhou immediately shouted and said, "Why, Senior, did you steal the monastery's fruit?
The monk said, "I have only just arrived; why do you say I stole the monastery's fruit? Muzhou said, "The stolen goods are right here before your eyes! The Master comments:
"Old Master Chen, I thought this was Muzhou’s own native land, but it turns out it is actually Puhua."
The official of the province asks: How do you know this? As soon as he opens his foul mouth, one sees his local dialect.
He thanks the new and old two classes of officials, as well as the West Hall Head Seat. The Abbot takes up the whisk and ascends the hall, addressing the assembly:
"Master Yuan of the Lotus Society had eighteen members who specifically purchased wine for Y渊明 (Tao Qian) to break their precepts; thus it has come down through the ages..."
This has become common talk on people’s lips; it is not only Master Yuanyang who holds this view.
Since I first sat upon my curved wooden seat, I have kept my mouth firmly sealed, vowing never to speak of worldly dharmas nor to speak of world-transcending dharmas. I maintain these two principles.
It has been more than ten years since [the community was established]. Now, we wish to renew the Dharma-society and restore the sagging discipline.

Since you, the venerable elders among the administrators, delight in preaching worldly dharmas, and having served as whisk-wielders for three great masters, you delight in preaching supramundane dharmas, I have therefore followed this path and broken my precepts to preach according to the needs of the occasion.
This is done with the hope that those who have already advanced will lend their hands to complete this work, and that those who have already retreated will likewise join us.
With your support, the collapsing discipline has now been restored and the Dharma community has been renewed.
Although this mountain monk’s sin of violating the precepts is certainly unavoidable, in the end, what constitutes worldly dharma and what constitutes world-transcending dharma?
What I have related previously is entirely the truth.

On the eighth day of the twelfth month, when ascending the hall, I cited from the sutra: "The path of the Buddha is vast and remote; only after enduring diligent suffering for a long time can it be accomplished."
Great assembly, Śākyamuni the Old Man is currently practicing; he is truly undergoing hardship. How can you see this? A single grain of hemp, a single grain of wheat;
the Snow Mountains are white and bright, yet he scatters stars before his eyes on the eighth day of the first lunar month.
The Small Sermon on New Year’s Eve: Northern Chan boils the ox of the open field, yet he cannot avoid wasting salt and vinegar;

Donglin burns firewood, which is more fitting for seeing out the old and welcoming the new. If you understand it in this way, you will sink into the mud on level ground; if you seek anything else besides this, you are merely adding further confusion.
Home grows ever more distant. We, this assembly of some two hundred, are all guests who have arrived home. In the morning we gaze upon the white clouds; in the evening we listen to the flowing water.
We eat rice from the fields and sleep upon long continuous beds. Who cares for you, the old fellow of the Yama family, with your hundreds of upright and thousands of horizontal rules?
Whether it be the new or the old Lord of the Year, jostling one another for precedence—every year is a good year, and every month is a good month.
The Moon. Every day is a good day; every moment is a good moment. Of all things that are good, there is none that is not good.
But ultimately, where does this goodness reside? Goodness—thirty blows of the staff!

On the first day of the New Year, he ascended the hall and addressed the assembly: "Venerable ones, this staff—just as the fifth watch bell struck this morning, it went to Nālandā Monastery in India to celebrate the New Year.
There it beheld a newly manifested Buddha appearing in the world to preach the Dharma of the New Year.

Having listened for a long time, it was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; returning before me on this mountain, it has raised it up several times in succession and continues to offer its praise with repeated voices."
I was born in this land long ago, yet I have never before heard such a subtle and profound essential teaching of the Dharma.
When I, this mountain monk, listened to it, it was indeed strange and marvelous. Among its phrases, there were some that resembled Sanskrit;
some that were like the language of Tang; and some that could not be translated into either Tang or Sanskrit. Alas for me, this mountain monk!... [text ends]
I have become quite forgetful; I cannot even remember a single word perfectly. Now, I must trouble you, Master of the Staff, to come forth and repeat it from the beginning for everyone.
You must also examine each point with clear discernment. (He strikes the staff once and says: "Can you discern it?
If you can discern it, then India and this land will be as one family. This year, go..."
Year after year, there is no difference at all. Should this not yet be so, there shall be new rules for the coming year; the spring wind that brings such vexation will never cease.

On the occasion of the Yuanxiao Festival, he ascended the hall and addressed the assembly: "When the Elder Śākyamuni saw Dīpaṃkara and personally received his prediction of enlightenment, it was as if he had never done so."
If you do not believe it, simply look at the true face of Mount Lu: layer upon layer, through mist and rain.
Ascending the hall, he cited Gushan’s address to the assembly, which said: "As for this matter, it is like a single sword. At that time, a monk came forward and asked:
"I have heard the Master's address to the assembly: 'As for this matter, it is like a single sword. But the Master himself is a corpse!"
"The student is a corpse. [The monk asked,] "Furthermore, what is the sword? Gushan said, "Drag out this corpse! The monk packed his bundle and departed immediately.
That evening, Gushan asked the Head Seat, "Is the monk who came to question me still here? The Head Seat replied, "He has already left.
Gushan said, "A fine thirty blows for him. The Master commented: "Gushan’s sword-spirit pierced the ox and the dipper (the heavens)."
This monk’s eyes have opened and a radiant light shines forth. Even so, were one to discuss this matter, it would take sixty kalpas across three lifetimes.
Entering the hall for the Buddha-bath ceremony: a blind owl in an eagle’s nest; a sharp falcon in a pigeon’s coop. To claim supremacy does not necessarily mean one is supreme; to act...
Small is not necessarily small; it is merely washing mud with mud. In the end, there is no clarity at all.
If there were clarity, the waters of the sea could not withstand being scooped up with a ladle.

Ascending the hall for the Summer Retreat. (Holding up the staff) Throughout the entire universe and great earth—whether sages or ordinary beings, sentient or insentient—(thrusting it down once) all dwell and enter retreat within this very place.
During these ninety days, you must by no means depart from here, nor must you remain fixedly attached to here. To depart from here would cause you to run wild; to remain fixedly attached...
If you turn inward, it will bind and kill you. Since you are not permitted to leave it behind, nor permitted to dwell upon it, how, in the end, can you turn yourself around?
Zhaozhou’s cassock weighs seven catties.
Ascending the hall: Ten days have passed since the summer retreat began. Day after day the sun rises in the east; yet Han Shan alone is difficult to find.
To the east he has left no trace; to the west there is no news. (Suddenly grasping the staff, he looks around and says:
"A dark, wrinkled thing seven feet long. (He strikes once. "In an ordinary moment, it cleaves through the rocks of a thousand crags."

Ascending the hall on the Double Fifth: The Double Fifth of the fifth month is a season of strict observance. The *ài* figures suffer from unremitting pain; alas, their illness has reached the depths of the gallbladder and the diaphragm.
Furthermore, they are deluded by malevolent spirits. To encounter the Great Lord Lao is likewise to encounter "red mouths and white tongues" (calumny).

I, this mountain monk, have reflected on this matter again and again; there is no other elixir or secret formula. Now, having no choice but to do so, I must simply "plunder" him right where he stands.
(He strikes the meditation staff once. He then ascends the hall and, for the sake of warming one particular point, cites the case of Nanquan when he was staying in a hermitage:
a monk arrived, and Nanquan said, "I am going up the mountain to work; please accept my invitation for a meal."
At that time, he prepared some food and ate it himself, saying, "Bring a portion for me. The monk finished his meal and then smashed all the household utensils at once;
he then lay down upon the bed. Nanquan waited for him to come, but when he returned and saw the monk lying on the bed, Nanquan also went and lay down on one side.
The monk then got up and left. After Nanquan took charge of the monastery, he said: "I..."
"When he first lived in the hermitage, there was a clever practitioner who has not been seen since. Xidang Xian took up the case, saying:
'How is it that Nanquan was deceived by this monk? Upon returning and seeing him lying there, Nanquan simply settled his affairs, prepared his own meal, and sat in meditation within the hut.
Let us just wait for this fellow to sleep himself to death. The Master commented: [This is] a commentary.
"Cloud: Hūṃ, hūṃ! Master Xian, what kind of mental activity is this?
Not only do you intend to 'sleep-kill' that fellow, but you also intend to 'sit-kill' Old Nanquan. Even so, you still cannot escape the entanglements of those ancients."
Having accepted the invitation from the Prince of Heaven (the Emperor), he faced the palace to express his gratitude.
Upon concluding this, he held up the imperial decree and said: "In the depths of the white clouds, it is good to sleep soundly; wild vegetables seasoned with oil have a long-lasting flavor."
The teaching-titles of Mount Kanglu remain vital through the ages; the mountain monk laughs as he tears open the fragrant purple clay seal.
Compiled by the attendants Zongqing, Jixian, and others, this is the *Recorded Sayings* of Tiantong Jingde Chan Temple at Taibai, a Famous Mountain in Qingyuan Prefecture.
On the fifteenth day of the eleventh month in the twelfth year of Chunyou, the Master entered the monastery. Pointing to the triple gate, he said:
"The entire universe and the great earth are all my gateway of great sovereign freedom for entering and exiting and playing at will.
The myriad phenomena and the vast array of forms are all my attendants. Do you believe this? I have come along with them."
The Buddha Hall—the nostrils of Old Śākyamuni—are right now in the hands of this mountain monk.
It has reached the point where all people throughout the entire world have nowhere to breathe. Now tell me: is this holding fast, or is it letting go? Xiao He established the laws;
the Duke of Zhou established the rites.
The Abbot: A net of raw iron spread over a net of silk. He picks it up and sets it against one wall. How magnificent! What a fine crew of living monks!
(He strikes the meditation seat once and says: Even they cannot leap beyond this.
Taking up the imperial decree, this very matter is truly unspeakable; within the unspeakable, it is truly speakable. Truly speakable...
To speak of the unspeakable. Teeth on edge, jaws clenched. Urgently command the gathering.
The Dharma-seat points upward; the path lies beneath one's feet. Just as one prepares to ask "How is it?", one is merely mimicking the gait of Tang in Handan.
Ascending the seat, he offered incense, saying: "This single offering of incense is respectfully presented to extend blessings to the present Emperor, for his person:

Portrait of Master Fuyuan Tie (Requested by the Great Patriarch Jixiang Shifa):

"Esoteric mantras are not Sanskrit; they are the Tang language. They consist of drumming on clay drums and singing songs that lack the five notes and six pitch-pipes.

There is no escape from one’s transgressions. Oṃ ci lin bu lin. Hurry!
[I] have donated money to build this pavilion at Shendu Temple (where the portraits of the Master and my own likeness are inscribed; we rest together beneath the pine trees and beg for your support).

the three thousand majestic etiquettes and eighty thousand subtle practices are all gateways to death for those who are dead men. If you are a living patch-robed monk—
Monk! The skull opens its living eyes; when the living eyes open, the great trichiliocosm is but a single speck of dust.

the one atop the city wall has entered the very marrow.

The Chan Master Zhen entered the very marrow [of his being] (he died of leprosy).
Between the Western Region of India and the Eastern Land of China, there is a public case (*gong'an*). To look at it is to lose all one's eyebrows;

the medicinal bag is already behind the funeral carriage.

Tenfold cold hues lock in the thousand peaks; the fire-pit with its firewood is warm and glowing.

The Recorded Sayings of Master Xiyuan, Scroll Lower (End). Biographical Account:

The Master’s name was Liaohui. He was a native of Pengchi in Pengzhou, Shu, and a son of the Luo family. Even when his hair hung down in locks, he would play with other children, yet [his conduct] was invariably...
He kneaded mud and sand to fashion the form of a Buddhist stupa. One day, the monk Zudeng from Anguo Temple on Mount Yupang came to his house;

the Master joined his palms toward him, and Deng patted his head, saying, "Do you wish to follow me? Because the karmic conditions between teacher and disciple had converged, the Master relied upon him as his patron and was subsequently permitted to leave the household life.
At nineteen, he shaved his hair, and Deng bestowed upon him the *Banzhou nianfo sanmei* (Pratyutpanna Samādhi of Buddha-Recitation).
This was not his true aspiration. He declined the invitation to the lecture seat in Chengdu and devoted himself to studying the sutras and śāstras of the Nature School (Xingzong).
Soon, he sighed, saying, "Scholastic study is surely not the ultimate Dharma; it is enough to have merely dipped one's finger in it. He departed to visit Huai’an Zhao at Zhaojue Temple.

Upon seeing him, Zhao recognized him at once as a vessel for the Dharma and urged him to travel south in search of instruction. Thereupon, he packed his bundle and emerged from the Three Gorges, traveling through Huxiang and reaching Jiangzhe.
He visited Master Zhe-weng Yan at Mount Jing and heard that Master Gao-yuan Quan was solitary, firm, and direct. He went to rely upon him, finding their shared austerity as sweet as molasses.
When Quan moved to Ruiyan on Mount Tai, he took the Master with him. Quan asked: "Mountains, rivers, and the great earth—"

"Is it existent? Is it non-existent? [The Master] was about to open his mouth, when [Master Quan] shouted at him and drove him out. He presented a verse, to which [Quan] immediately replied, "There is no connection.
Later, while serving [Quan], [the Master] was ordered to transcribe the "Three Self-Reflections of Longmen" and the words of Baiyang shown to the assembly.

Upon reading them, Quan laughed and said, "How can writing characters ever suffice for composing speech? Yet, what can one do about there being no connection? The Master was frustrated and unable to express himself; Quan said, "I—"
The expedient means were already prepared; it was simply that you did not take heed yourself, as the Dharma was not present there. Why not go and visit Xuedou?
At that time, the one presiding over the seat at Xuedou was Foguan Wuzhun Fan. The Master went to the assembly hall and personally recounted his background.
Fan scolded him, saying, "Go and rest thoroughly. Subsequently, he appointed Chong as an attendant who did not handle administrative affairs, telling him:

"The place where you cannot see through lies right at the tip of your nose; when you cannot speak it, it does not leave your lips. When Chong sought it, it seemed a thousand or ten thousand miles away.
The Master raised his voice and said, "I thought there was so much to it! Later, when Fan moved to Yuyang Monastery, the Master accompanied him on his travels.

In his daily life he was composed and at ease; thus he finally exhausted the essentials [of the Way]. Next, he met Shitian Xun, who marveled at him upon their conversation. He also met Miaofeng Shan at Wanshou Monastery in Wumen.
Shan asked, "Where have you recently departed from? He replied, "Jingci. Shan asked, "What sayings or phrases did Jingci use to instruct his disciples?
He replied, "He gave a fine formal lecture (shangtang). Shan asked, "How so? He replied, "I will relate it to you on another day. And so he did.
Shangshan said with a good laugh, "This monk from Guishan is not like others. At that time, Shoufan had already received an imperial decree to move to Mount Jing;
the Master went to visit him, and Shoufan immediately retained him, appointing him to serve as a model for the community. He was promoted from the position of Librarian to the Second Seat.

Many monasteries in the Wu region were occupied by the incompetent and the unworthy; it happened that Zhao Guanwen, the Marquis of Jiezhai, was serving as the Governor (Wenchang) at the time. The incompetent...
Zi waited for the wind [of the Master’s arrival] and withdrew, leaving his seat vacant for nineteen years. He gathered monks from various mountains and selected those of authentic character.

When the Master appeared in the world at Dinghui Temple, he offered a single incense stick for the sake of Fojian, recognizing what had been attained. The temple was cramped, dilapidated, and neglected;

it was repaired, patched, and renovated until it was entirely renewed, and only then did disciples begin to pass through its gates. Finding the bustle of the marketplace increasingly distasteful, he encountered the local authorities who came to...

The temple officials interrogated him, but he struck them back with vigor and would not allow himself to be detained. He returned to Shuangjing, where he swept his room clean and lived in serene self-contentment.
The Magistrate of Dongjia, Grand Supervisor Liu, invited him to the Nengren Temple; he resided there for three years.

Since the temple had been ravaged by fire thirty years prior, the monks' hall remained in a state of ruin and neglect. The Master initiated the effort to raise funds through the distribution of robes and alms bowls to undertake this reconstruction.

The retired official provided assistance, and various donors delighted in their charity; before long, the project was completed. The practice of Chan became profound and serene, and the ritual for the vegetarian feast was detailed and orderly;

the Chan monastery finally attained its full form. Suddenly, however, the Master sought to retire. Though those both within and without earnestly entreated him to stay, the Master said, "I originally set a term of three years.
Now that the assembly’s efforts have brought it to completion and we have fortunately reached this point, my impulse to depart cannot be restrained. [He then left for] Shixi at Lingyin.
Yue Shu invited him, and he crossed the river with effortless grace. Yue offered him the position of First Seat, but he did not accept.

When Yue was transferred to Mount Jing, Da Chuan Ji succeeded him on the seat; Yue invited [the Master] once more, yet he again declined. Provincial Governor Zhu of Jiangxi requested that Mount Jing recommend someone capable for Donglin; Yue recommended his teacher.
Zhu received him with great courtesy, but the Master said, "Mount Lu has long been a vast reservoir of Chan; though it is currently quiet..."
Liao. The famous mountains and waters remain intact; this journey shall allow you to fulfill your long-cherished vow. After residing there for one year, the seat at Tiantong became vacant.

By imperial decree, various Chan masters were summoned, and the Master’s name was submitted for recommendation. He was specially appointed to fill the position. Over the course of five years, he trained his disciples and restored what had fallen into ruin, applying himself with unremitting care.
The two pavilions, one after the other, rose gold and azure toward the heavens. Furthermore, he intended to expand the "Selection of Buddhas" (the monastic examinations).
The site was renovated anew. Yet, when the fire-god Huilu (Agni) fanned the flames, half the work was destroyed in a single day. Is this not destiny?
The Master remained equanimous amidst adversity and did not relax his rigorous regulations because of the disaster. The monks could not bear to abandon him;

Zongqing, Deyuan, Zhizhi, Yueyue, and others took up positions along the roads to beg for alms to assist in the restoration. They first renovated the Candana-vana (Zhantanlin), followed by the administrative offices, the kitchen, and the corridors.
The quarters were also completed in succession. Having already selected the timber for the Water and Land Hall (Shuilu-tang), he suddenly fell ill.

He submitted a leave of absence to the Imperial Commissioner Lüzhai (履齋) Wu Gong, who appointed Zhizou of Mount Jiangshan, Beishan (別山), to succeed him in the seat; they were close friends within the Dharma.
The Master retired to sweep his single mat at Mount Zhongfeng for three years. Zhao Daqing of Songhe came to visit and said, "Ruian Rock..."

The late Master, King Cheongmin, had already ascended to the realm of the spirits; how could it be appropriate for one of such renowned virtue to preside over this place by occupying its high seat? He declined the offer.
Although the request was pressed with great persistence, he remained there for barely two years when his illness recurred. The Master said, "My worldly karmic ties have come to an end."

He retired to raise his ailment at the Qīngfēng Ŏu (Clear Wind Valley) Huànzhì Tà'ān (Illusory Wisdom Stūpa Hermitage). His disciples pooled their resources to complete the master’s [stūpa] as planned in previous years;

suddenly, they requested the inventory of his robes and bowl. The Master wrote a long inscription upon it and sealed it to be delivered to the temple officials, urging them to prepare for his final affairs.
When the disciples presented paper and requested a verse, the Master laughed and said, "This is not something I would do."
He then wrote: "If I were to leave behind verses for the various quarters, I would be ridiculed by the world; I must not allow myself to be ridiculed by the various quarters because of this.
He then cast aside his brush and, looking at those around him, asked, "What time is it now? They replied, "It is the second watch. He relaxed his body as if falling into deep sleep.
When they looked at him, he had already passed away. This was the twenty-second day of the third month in the third year of the Jingding era.
He lived to the age of sixty-five and sat in meditation for forty-seven summer retreats. His remains were left in his hermitage, while funeral rites were conducted at the monastery for five days.
The assembly enshrined his entire body in a stupa. He ordained several disciples, among whom those who inherited the Dharma appeared both before and after him.

Both teacher and disciples possessed keen faculties; his physical frame was slender and refined. Even in his prime, he relied on a staff as he traveled to visit various masters with singular determination. Regarding the vehicle of the school...
This matter was likely due to his former habits. Although he pained himself to remain in profound seclusion, his reputation and brilliance shone brightly.
When his karmic conditions matured and he responded to the world, he became an object of reverence and affection for the scholar-officials (*jinshen*) and was highly esteemed by his contemporaries.

Regarding the project to renovate the Sangha Hall at Nengren Monastery in Dongjia, there is a verse which says: "The Venerable One cast down his bowl from the void; though his spiritual powers were fully exhausted, it was nonetheless accomplished."
"Stupefied! Looking at him, he does not seem like the Elder Vimalakīrti; yet with one silence, a thousand gates and ten thousand doors open.
Chen Wenchang of Jiezhai, a guest official, was moved by this resonance upon first seeing him, and likewise offered elegant words to assist in the transformation: 'A venerable one from Jambudvīpa.'"
A single cloud and a single rain pervade the world. This morning, for the sake of the assembly, he entered the city. A fine drizzle followed him as he scattered across the spring fields.
Where there is a field but no rain, the harvest is not gathered; where there is a monk but no hall, the monk cannot remain.

Now that the monks have their hall and the fields have received rain, they cover three hundred prefectures from the southeast. Because of this, donors respond in kind, and thus [the temple] was swiftly completed. The Master.
Regarding practical achievements, one should act with diligence on what ought to be done, rather than striving for ostentation or extravagance.
As for his aspirations, they were focused solely on propagating the Way for the sake of others. At the gate of Fojian, talents gathered in great numbers; among them was the Master.
One might say he was truly one who could break firewood and carry burdens. I, Guan, first shared a seat with him among the assembly of elders.

Later, when I followed circumstances to East Zhejiang, we again shared the light of a neighboring candle. When his end drew near, he exerted himself despite his illness, leaning against his couch and composing five final letters.
I, Guan, am deeply indebted to him. Now his disciples, Zhichao and Zhihuan, came to my door weeping and said:

Because of our long-standing friendship, I could not decline; thus, I have set forth [the account] directly.

Nevertheless, the Buddha was distant from the Central Kingdom, separated by snow-capped peaks and deserts across more than a hundred thousand *li*. As for the extent of the transformation through Chan and the teachings...

The mechanisms prepared by the state are all dependent upon the timing of the era. Although the light was concealed beneath the *śāla* trees for over a thousand years, it took another five hundred years for the Great Teaching to gradually flow eastward until the orthodox lineage arrived in succession.
Had this not been so, how could the people have been matured and guided by the vehicles of the Dharma?

Yet when the orthodox lineage arrived suddenly, it was like a thunderclap from a clear blue sky; how could it not have caused shock and wonder at that time? From the Liang dynasty until the rise of the Song, many years had passed.

At Mount Yi-xiang-gong Lingxiao, he demonstrated his remembrance of his origins. I venture to say that while the study of names and forms flourished there as it did in the Song dynasty, the transmission of the orthodox lineage first took its initial signs with Jue’uo.

This is indeed the power [of the Dharma]. One shall witness a single lamp transmitting the lamp of infinity, its brilliance illuminating the world so that there is no night.

this may truly be called knowing where one’s direction lies. I, Yuan, reflect deeply upon the virtue and kindness of my late teacher, yet not even a single hair’s breadth of it has been repaid.
